134.title: Angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2)
134.hook: welcome strangers; some have hosted angels without knowing
134.howItsDone: Many Christians practice hospitality by welcoming visitors at church, opening their homes for meals, and hosting travelers; many monasteries keep guesthouses where anyone may stay, following Saint Benedict's rule to receive guests as Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday: alms, gifts to the poor, given without a trumpet. Your line was let it stay secret. Did you manage one quiet gift, and not tell anyone? Day one hundred thirty-four.

It's the hottest part of the day. An old man is sitting in the doorway of his tent, the kind of heat where nobody moves. He looks up and there are three strangers standing nearby. He doesn't wait for them to ask. He runs. An old man, running in that heat. He bows, begs them to stay, fetches water to wash their feet, tells his wife to bake bread from the good flour, picks out a calf himself. He calls it a little bread. It's a feast. He stands under a tree while they eat. The man is Abraham, in Genesis chapter eighteen, and before the day is over he learns who his guests really were. Centuries later, a letter in the New Testament remembers that afternoon. Today's word is what Abraham did.
screen: `THE HOTTEST PART OF THE DAY.` → `THREE STRANGERS.` → `ABRAHAM RUNS.`

segments.voice: Hospitality. In the New Testament the Greek word is philoxenia. Philo, love. Xenos, stranger. Love of the stranger. Not love of your friends, which is easy, but of the person you don't know yet. The letter to the Hebrews, near its end, gives a short list of how to live, and this is on it. In the King James Bible: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Unawares. Without knowing. Most readers hear Abraham in that line: the visitors at his tent turn out to be messengers of God, and in the story one of them promises that old Sarah will have a son. Abraham didn't welcome them because they were angels. He welcomed them, and they turned out to be. That's the order. In the ancient world this was not a small courtesy. There were no hotels for ordinary people. A traveler without a door to knock on could go hungry or be robbed. Opening your door could save a life, and it could cost you. Christians carried the practice forward. Jesus says in Matthew that at the end, the king will say: "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." Around fifteen hundred years ago, Saint Benedict wrote in his rule for monks that every guest should be welcomed as if Christ himself had come. Many monasteries still keep a guesthouse because of that line. Jews treasure the same story; welcoming guests is a commandment many Jewish families take to heart, and Abraham's open tent is its picture. So the idea is simple, and harder than it sounds: the person at your door might carry more than you can see.
screen: `PHILOXENIA — LOVE OF THE STRANGER.` · `SOME HAVE ENTERTAINED ANGELS.` · `A DOOR COULD SAVE A LIFE.` · `EVERY GUEST AS CHRIST.` · then, large: `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YE TOOK ME IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle and breathe. Picture your own door: your apartment, your desk at work, your spot in the cafeteria. Who comes to it that you barely notice? The delivery driver. The new person on the team. The neighbor you've nodded at for two years. Pick one face. Now imagine offering them something small to drink: water, a coffee, a cold soda on a hot day. Just that. If you pray, you can ask to see that person clearly. If you don't, simply hold their face for a moment with a little more warmth than usual. The bell holds the time.
Hospitality. In Greek, philoxenia, love of the stranger. Abraham ran to his guests before he knew who they were.
Your line: strangers might be angels. Today, offer one guest or visitor something to drink, and see who they turn out to be. Day one hundred thirty-four.

fork.reveal: he runs, in the heat of the day, and serves them a feast he calls a little bread. only later does he learn who his guests were.

what it means: welcoming the stranger, the one you don't know yet, as if they might carry more than you can see.
what a scholar hears: philoxenia. xenos means both stranger and guest, and in a world without inns, hospitality was a matter of life and safety.

135.title: The church sings (Colossians 3:16)
135.hook: the first Christians sang psalms, hymns and spiritual songs
135.howItsDone: Nearly every Christian church sings when it gathers: Orthodox and many Catholic services chant much of the liturgy, and Protestant congregations sing hymns and worship songs together, often with an organ, piano or band.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hospitality, love of the stranger, and Abraham running to three guests in the heat. Your line was strangers might be angels. Who did you offer a drink to? Day one hundred thirty-five.

Midnight in a prison in the city of Philippi. Two men, Paul and Silas, have been beaten with rods and locked in the inner cell, their feet fastened in stocks. Their backs are bleeding. The other prisoners are in the dark around them, and you can imagine what that dark sounds like. And then, from the inner cell, something nobody expects. Singing. The book of Acts says it plainly: at midnight they prayed and sang praises to God, and the prisoners heard them. Not after they were freed. Before. In the stocks. It's one of the oldest pictures we have of Christians doing what they have done in every century since, in cathedrals, in basements, in fields: when they gather, they sing. Today, the church sings.
screen: `MIDNIGHT IN PHILIPPI.` → `FEET IN THE STOCKS.` → `THEY SANG, AND THE PRISONERS HEARD.`

segments.voice: The church sang from the very first night. The Gospel of Mark says that after the last supper, before they walked out to the Mount of Olives, Jesus and his friends sang: "And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives." Many scholars think it was psalms that Jews sang at Passover, the ones still sung at the Passover table today. So the church's first song was a Jewish song. Then Paul, writing to the Christians in Colossae, describes what their gatherings sounded like. In the King James Bible: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." Psalms, hymns, spiritual songs. Nobody knows exactly where one ends and the next begins. Psalms likely means the old songs of Israel. Hymns, songs of praise. Spiritual songs might be something newer, even made up in the moment. Notice who's teaching whom: one another. Singing was how they taught. A tune carries words into memory in a way a lecture can't. And outsiders noticed. Around the year 112, a Roman governor named Pliny wrote to the emperor about these odd people called Christians. He reported that they met before dawn on a fixed day and sang a hymn to Christ, as to a god. A Roman official, not a friend, is one of our earliest witnesses that they sang. Today's line, who sings prays twice, is often credited to Saint Augustine. Scholars can't find those exact words in his writings. But he did write about weeping when he heard the church sing. The idea stuck because so many people recognize it: when you sing a prayer, your breath and your body pray it too.
screen: `THEY SANG AN HYMN, AND WENT OUT.` · `PSALMS, HYMNS, SPIRITUAL SONGS.` · `SINGING WAS HOW THEY TAUGHT.` · `A ROMAN HEARD THEM BEFORE DAWN.` · then, large: `WHO SINGS PRAYS TWICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. You don't need a good voice. You barely need a voice at all. Think of one line of a hymn or church song you know, any one. Amazing grace. Holy, holy, holy. Jesus loves me. If none come to mind, hum a tune you remember from a wedding or a funeral. Breathe in, and sing or hum that one line, softly, once. Then again, slower. Notice where the sound sits in your chest. If you pray, let the line be your prayer. If you don't, just notice what a song does to your breath. The bell holds the time.
The church sings. From the upper room to a prison at midnight, Christians have always gathered with psalms, hymns and spiritual songs.
Your line: who sings prays twice. Today, sing or hum one line of a hymn, in the shower, in the car, under your breath. Day one hundred thirty-five.

fork.reveal: at midnight Paul and Silas prayed and sang praises to God, and the prisoners heard them. the song came before the rescue, not after.

136.title: Watts and Wesley
136.hook: two Englishmen wrote thousands of hymns still sung, like When I Survey and And Can It Be
136.howItsDone: Many churches sing hymns by Isaac Watts and Charles Wesley from printed hymnals or screens, especially at Christmas, Easter and funerals, and some Christians read hymns privately as poems or prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the church sings, from the upper room to a prison cell at midnight. Your line was who sings prays twice. Did one line of a song escape you? Day one hundred thirty-six.

England, around three hundred years ago. A teenager named Isaac Watts sits in church, and he is bored. Back then, most English churches sang only the psalms, set into stiff rhymes, lined out one line at a time by a leader and dragged back by the congregation. The story goes that young Isaac complained, and his father said, more or less: then write something better. So he did. Not one hymn. Hundreds. Some of them are still sung every Christmas and every Good Friday. A generation later, a restless Anglican priest named Charles Wesley would write thousands more. Between them, these two men taught the English-speaking church a new way to sing. Today's word is what they wrote.
screen: `A BORED TEENAGER IN CHURCH.` → `THEN WRITE SOMETHING BETTER.` → `HUNDREDS, THEN THOUSANDS.`

segments.voice: Hymn. From the Greek hymnos, a song of praise to a god or a hero. For Christians, a hymn is a song of praise written in verses, sung by the whole congregation. Isaac Watts did something that sounds simple now and was daring then. He wrote new songs in plain English, in the voice of the people singing them, about the gospel. People call him the father of English hymnody. He wrote Joy to the World. He wrote O God, Our Help in Ages Past. And he wrote the one many call the finest hymn in English, When I Survey the Wondrous Cross, from 1707. It walks slowly toward the cross, looks, and ends with a line that turned into today's carry: "Love so amazing, so divine, Demands my soul, my life, my all." Read it again as a poem, and notice it doesn't argue. It just looks and answers. Then Charles Wesley. He and his brother John started the movement that became the Methodists, and Charles wrote verse almost every day of his life, somewhere around six thousand hymns. Hark! the Herald Angels Sing. Love Divine, All Loves Excelling. And And Can It Be, written around the time of his own conversion in 1738. It is full of astonishment: "Amazing love! How can it be That Thou, my God, shouldst die for me?" One man a careful poet, the other a fountain. Watts was a Congregationalist; Wesley an Anglican. Today they're sung by Baptists, Catholics, Lutherans, Pentecostals and everyone between. Both keep landing on the same astonished word: amazing. A hymn is theology you can sing, in words plain enough that a tired congregation can carry it home.
screen: `HYMNOS — A SONG OF PRAISE.` · `WATTS: WHEN I SURVEY, 1707.` · `WESLEY: SIX THOUSAND HYMNS.` · `THEOLOGY YOU CAN SING.` · then, large: `LOVE SO AMAZING, SO DIVINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a hymn verse as a poem. Take the last verse of When I Survey. Say it slowly, not sung, just spoken, with a pause at every comma. "Were the whole realm of nature mine, That were a present far too small; Love so amazing, so divine, Demands my soul, my life, my all." Now sit with it. Which word catches? Realm. Small. Demands. Let it catch. If you pray, you can pray it back slowly. If you don't, just read it as what it is: a man looking at something and finding his hands empty. The bell holds the time.
Hymn. From the Greek hymnos, a song of praise. A poem in verses, made for a whole congregation to sing.
Your line: love so amazing. Today, look up one hymn by Watts or Wesley and read a single verse slowly, like a poem. Day one hundred thirty-six.

fork.reveal: the story goes that young Isaac Watts did exactly that, and kept going for hundreds of hymns. the story is told often; the details are hard to confirm.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn is any old church song.
what it means: a poem of praise in verses, written for a whole congregation to sing, theology plain enough to carry home.

137.title: The spirituals
137.hook: enslaved Africans in America made songs of Moses, Jordan and freedom that carried hope and plans
137.howItsDone: Spirituals are sung in many Black churches and in churches of every kind, by choirs and congregations, and are often sung in services remembering freedom, justice and the civil rights movement.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the hymn, and two Englishmen, Watts and Wesley. Your line was love so amazing. Did you read one verse slowly, like a poem? Day one hundred thirty-seven.

A field in the American South, before the Civil War. The sun is brutal and the work doesn't stop. Enslaved men and women are forbidden to read, often forbidden to gather, and sold away from their own children. And out in that field, someone starts a song. When Israel was in Egypt's land. Others answer: let my people go. To the overseer on his horse, it might sound like an old Bible story. To the people singing, it was about them. About Pharaoh, and chains, and a God who hears slaves and takes their side. Some of these songs carried hope. Some, people say, carried plans. Today's word is the name for these songs, which may be the most important music America ever made.
screen: `A FIELD BEFORE THE CIVIL WAR.` → `WHEN ISRAEL WAS IN EGYPT'S LAND.` → `A BIBLE STORY, OR THEIR STORY?`

segments.voice: Spiritual. A religious folk song made by enslaved Africans in America, mostly in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Nobody knows who wrote most of them. They grew the way folk songs grow: sung, changed, passed on. Listen to what they chose to sing about. Moses and Pharaoh. The river Jordan. Daniel in the lions' den. The chariot coming for me. They took the Exodus and put themselves inside it. In the book of Exodus, in the King James Bible, Moses walks into Pharaoh's court and says: "Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Let my people go." The spiritual made that line a refrain: "When Israel was in Egypt's land, Let my people go." You didn't need to spell out who Pharaoh was. Now the question of plans. Frederick Douglass, who escaped slavery, wrote that when they sang about reaching Canaan, some of them meant the North. So yes, some songs held double meanings. Harriet Tubman, who led people out of slavery, was called the Moses of her people, and an early biography says she used songs as signals. But historians are careful here. Some famous claims, like songs that were secret maps, are hard to prove, and a few were written down only much later. What's certain is this: these songs were faith and resistance at the same time, and nobody had to choose between them. After the war, in 1871, a small group of students from Fisk University, a new school for freed people, went on tour to save it from debt. They sang spirituals, for audiences who had never heard them sung like that, even for Queen Victoria. The Fisk Jubilee Singers carried these songs to the world.
screen: `SONGS WITH NO KNOWN AUTHOR.` · `THEY PUT THEMSELVES IN EXODUS.` · `HOPE, AND SOMETIMES PLANS.` · `FISK, 1871: SONGS TO THE WORLD.` · then, large: `LET MY PEOPLE GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one spiritual you know, even a scrap of it. Go down, Moses. Swing low, sweet chariot. Wade in the water. Deep river. Hum it if it comes, or just remember its shape. Then think about who first sang it: people with every reason to despair, singing about a God who sets slaves free. Let that sit with you for a minute. If you pray, you can hold in prayer anyone who is not free today. If you don't, just hold them in mind. Later, listen to one spiritual all the way through. The bell holds the time.
Spiritual. A song of faith made by enslaved Africans in America, full of Moses, Jordan and freedom.
Your line: let my people go. Today, listen to one spiritual, start to finish, and notice the Bible story inside it. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

options: the popular songs of the day.

fork.reveal: the Fisk Jubilee Singers sang spirituals, and audiences across America and Europe had never heard anything like it. the tour saved the school.

trapdoor: what you thought: spirituals are old church songs.
what it means: songs made by enslaved people who put themselves inside the Exodus: faith and resistance at once.
what a scholar hears: an oral tradition, mostly unwritten until the 1860s. the Fisk Jubilee Singers, from 1871, brought arranged spirituals to concert halls around the world.

138.title: Holy, holy, holy
138.hook: Orthodox churches sing Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us
138.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians sing the Trisagion in the Divine Liturgy and pray it three times at the start of daily prayers, often making the sign of the cross each time; Catholics sing it on Good Friday, and many churches sing Isaiah's 'Holy, holy, holy' at communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the spiritual, songs of Moses and Jordan made by people who were not free. Your line was let my people go. Which song did you listen to? Day one hundred thirty-eight.

Walk into an Orthodox church on a Sunday morning. Candles, icons, incense hanging in the air, and very likely no pews, just people standing. At a certain point in the service, the choir begins a short chant, and the whole church seems to lean into it. Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us. Then again. And again. Three times, sometimes more, slow enough that the words have room. It's so short you could learn it on the way home. It's so old that people were singing it before most of Europe's cathedrals were built. Today's word is its name, and it comes from a vision a prophet had in the Temple.
screen: `CANDLES, ICONS, INCENSE.` → `HOLY GOD, HOLY MIGHTY, HOLY IMMORTAL.` → `THREE TIMES, SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Trisagion. Greek: tris, three times, and hagion, holy. The thrice-holy. Its roots go back to the prophet Isaiah. In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the Lord on a throne, high and lifted up, and fiery creatures called seraphim calling to one another. The King James Bible gives their words: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Why three times? In Hebrew, saying a word twice makes it strong. Three times is as strong as it gets. Holiest. Beyond everything. At the end of the Bible, in Revelation, the song is still going: creatures around the throne "rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come." The Trisagion takes that cry and turns it into three lines people can pray: Holy God. Holy Mighty. Holy Immortal. And then one very human request: have mercy on us. Nobody knows for certain who first put it together. There's a story people tell, from Constantinople in the fifth century, of an earthquake, and a boy caught up into the sky who heard angels singing it. What we do know is that it was being sung by 451, at a great council of bishops. Orthodox Christians sing it in nearly every service and pray it at home to begin their prayers. Catholics sing it too, in Greek and Latin, on Good Friday. Many Christians of other churches sing Isaiah's three holies every Sunday, in the Holy, Holy, Holy of the communion service, or in the nineteenth-century hymn of the same name. The pattern holds in all of them: first praise beyond words, then a plea for mercy, close to the ground.
screen: `TRIS, HAGION — THRICE HOLY.` · `ISAIAH SEES THE SERAPHIM.` · `THREE TIMES MEANS HOLIEST.` · `PRAISE FIRST, THEN MERCY.` · then, large: `HOLY GOD, HOLY MIGHTY, HOLY IMMORTAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit or stand, whichever you like; many Orthodox Christians stand to pray. Breathe in, and out. If you pray, you can say the Trisagion three times, slowly, one line per breath. Holy God. Holy Mighty. Holy Immortal. Have mercy on us. If you don't pray, you can simply say the words as words, and notice the shape: something vast, and then something small asking for mercy. After the third time, let the silence hold. The bell holds the time.
Trisagion. The thrice-holy. An ancient chant from Isaiah's vision: Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us.
Your line: holy, holy, holy. Today, when something stops you in your tracks, a sky, a face, a piece of music, let those three words come. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

139.title: Gospel, Taizé and worship songs
139.hook: from Black gospel choirs to Taizé's repeated chants to modern worship bands
139.howItsDone: Christians sing in many styles: gospel choirs in many Black churches, Taizé chants at prayer services across denominations, contemporary worship bands in many Protestant churches, and unaccompanied chant in Orthodox and some Protestant churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Trisagion, holy, holy, holy, and then a plea for mercy. And this whole week: the tithe, the widow's coins, alms, a stranger's welcome, and then the church singing. Today the week ends with music. Day one hundred thirty-nine.
screen: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` → `A WEEK OF GIVING AND SINGING.`

segments.voice: Three rooms, one Sunday. In the first, a choir in bright robes is swaying, a Hammond organ is growling, and a soloist holds one note until the whole church is on its feet. In the second, a stone village church in France, thousands of young people are sitting on the floor in candlelight, singing the same short phrase over and over, quieter each time, until it feels like breathing. In the third, a converted warehouse, the lights go low, a drummer counts in, and a band plays while people raise their hands. Three sounds that could hardly be more different. And people in all three rooms would tell you the same thing: we were praying. Today's word names the first of them.
screen: `A CHOIR AND A HAMMOND ORGAN.` → `CANDLES AND ONE PHRASE, REPEATED.` → `A BAND IN A WAREHOUSE.`

segments.voice: Gospel. The word means good news, and it names a kind of music born in Black churches in America. It grew out of the spirituals we met two days ago, the blues and the energy of Pentecostal worship. The man often called its father is Thomas A. Dorsey, a Chicago blues pianist. In 1932 his wife died giving birth, and their baby son died soon after. In that grief, he sat down at a piano and wrote Take My Hand, Precious Lord. Mahalia Jackson sang it across the world, and it was sung at Martin Luther King Junior's funeral. Gospel music often comes out of the hardest places. Taizé is something else. It's a small community of brothers in a village in France, begun by Brother Roger in 1940, with members from Protestant and Catholic churches together. Every week, young people come by the thousands. Their songs are short: one line of scripture or prayer, sung again and again, sometimes in Latin, sometimes in many languages. The repetition is the point. By the tenth time you stop thinking about the words and start praying them. Then modern worship music, from the late twentieth century on: guitars, drums, songs sung straight to God, now heard in churches everywhere. Not every church uses instruments. Many Orthodox churches sing without them, and some Protestant churches, like the Churches of Christ, sing unaccompanied on purpose. Others use every instrument they can find, because the last psalm says, in the King James Bible: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Christians argue about music, sometimes loudly. But a choir, a chant and a band can all carry the same prayer.
screen: `GOSPEL: BORN IN BLACK CHURCHES.` · `DORSEY: PRECIOUS LORD, 1932.` · `TAIZÉ: ONE LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `WITH INSTRUMENTS, OR WITHOUT.` · then, large: `LET EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. This week you've given in secret, welcomed a stranger, and sung. Now just listen. Settle, and breathe. Think of the style of church music that feels least like you: the gospel choir, the quiet chant, the loud band, the old organ. Imagine yourself in that room for a minute. Imagine the person next to you, for whom this is exactly how prayer sounds. Let yourself be curious rather than critical. If you pray, you can pray alongside them in your mind. Later today, listen to one piece of church music, any style. The bell holds the time.
Gospel. Good news, and a music born in Black churches in America, where grief and joy share one song.
Your line: every style can pray. Today, listen to one piece of church music, maybe in a style you'd never choose. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

140.title: Fellowship (Acts 2:42)
140.hook: the first believers devoted themselves to teaching, fellowship, bread and prayers
140.carry: you weren't meant to do it alone
140.howItsDone: Many churches keep fellowship through shared meals, coffee after services, home groups and collections for people in need, and many Christians take Acts 2:42 as a picture of what church life should include.

segments.voice: Yesterday: gospel, Taizé and the worship band, three rooms praying in three sounds. Your line was every style can pray. Did you listen to something new? A new week starts now: together and alone. Day one hundred forty.
screen: `EVERY STYLE CAN PRAY.` → `A NEW WEEK: TOGETHER AND ALONE.`

segments.voice: Jerusalem, a few weeks after Easter. Something has happened at Pentecost, and suddenly there are thousands of new believers where there were barely a hundred. No church buildings. No clergy training. No plan. What do they actually do, day to day? The book of Acts gives a snapshot, and it's surprisingly ordinary. They listen to the apostles teach. They eat together in each other's homes. They pray. They share what they have, so nobody goes without. It reads less like the founding of a religion and more like a very large family learning to live together. And tucked in the middle of that list is a Greek word the church has never stopped using. Today's word.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF NEW BELIEVERS.` → `NO BUILDINGS, NO PLAN.` → `THEY ATE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Koinonia. It comes from koinos, common, shared, what belongs to everyone. So koinonia is having something in common: partnership, participation, sharing. English usually translates it fellowship, which is fine, but it's thicker than coffee after church. Here's the verse, in the King James Bible: "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." Four things. Teaching, fellowship, bread, prayers. Churches still use that verse as a checklist. Now watch how the same word gets used elsewhere in the New Testament. Paul uses koinonia for money: a collection the churches took up for poor believers in Jerusalem. Sharing your wallet is koinonia. He uses it for the bread and cup: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?" That word communion is koinonia. And he uses it for sharing in someone's suffering. So one word covers a meal, a bank transfer, the Lord's Supper and a hard season. That tells you what the first Christians thought church was. Not an event you attend. A life you share. Acts says they ate their meals with gladness. There's a line in Genesis, right at the start, that sits underneath all this: "It is not good that the man should be alone." Christians have many ways of living it out. Some churches keep a meal after every service. Orthodox and Catholic Christians speak of the whole church, living and dead, sharing one communion. Many Protestants meet in homes midweek. Different forms, one conviction: faith was never meant to be carried solo.
screen: `KOINOS — COMMON, SHARED.` · `TEACHING, FELLOWSHIP, BREAD, PRAYERS.` · `A MEAL, MONEY, THE CUP, SUFFERING.` · `A LIFE YOU SHARE.` · then, large: `IT IS NOT GOOD THAT THE MAN SHOULD BE ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Picture the last meal you shared with someone, really shared, not just ate near. Where were you? What did you talk about? Now let a face come to mind: someone you haven't eaten with in too long. A friend, a neighbor, a parent, someone who might be lonelier than they let on. Hold that face for a minute. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just wish them well. Then decide: a meal, a coffee, even a sandwich on a bench, this week. The bell holds the time.
Koinonia. Greek for sharing a common life. Fellowship, communion, partnership: a meal, a purse and a faith held together.
Your line: you weren't meant to do it alone. Today, share a meal with someone, or set a date to. Day one hundred forty.
